item.title: When Violence Is the Point
item.description:
Law and Crime

When Violence Is the Point

Nihilistic violent extremism is spreading. Experts can’t agree on what it is.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Online networks are grooming teenagers into self-harm, sexual exploitation, and violence as a path to status.
  • Experts largely agree that misanthropy and clout-chasing sit at the core of nihilistic violent extremism.
  • They still disagree about ideology, the purpose of the violence, copycatting, and the label’s boundaries.

By Avery Ellis and H. Colleen Sinclair, Ph.D.

On January 4, 2025, a 14-year-old boy in Borås, Sweden, walked up to a 55-year-old woman who was out walking her dog and stabbed her. He streamed the attack live on Discord to an online group he desperately wanted to join.

The attack wasn’t his idea. The group first gave him an initiation task: Slash car tires. When he did, they told him it wasn’t enough. Find a human target, they said. The woman survived after two surgeries. Streaming viewers tipped off police, who arrested the boy that evening. When asked why he did it, he said he wanted to belong.

Was this extremism? A random assault? A gang initiation? Child exploitation? Unsettlingly, it may be all four. U.S. law enforcement has a name for this kind of threat: nihilistic violent extremism, or NVE, a label the FBI and Department of Justice introduced in 2025. It describes loosely connected online networks, many of them branching out of a sprawling ecosystem called the Com (short for “the community”).

This ecosystem is also linked to TCC, the “True Crime Community,” dark fandoms (soon to be featured on 60 Minutes). But unlike the images that the TCC descriptor might bring to mind of keyboard sleuths obsessed with crime documentaries, these individuals are more interested in committing than solving crime. Their modus operandi is recruiting young people through gaming platforms and social media sites to push them toward harming themselves and others. It is grooming for violence.

The threat is growing fast. The Polarization and Extremism Research and Innovation Lab (PERIL) counted eight NVE-linked plots and attacks worldwide in 2023. By mid-November 2026, it had counted 69 for the year, an increase of 763 percent (Jensen, 2026). Schools were the most common target, and outside the United States, the median perpetrator age was just 16.

These threats take more than one form. Just this month, Bavarian authorities arrested two teenagers from the German state of Hesse. They are suspected members of the Com who pressured three girls aged 13 and 14 into filming sexual acts and self-harm (News.de, 2026).

A stabbing in Sweden and online sextortion in Germany look like very different crimes, yet both fall under the same label. That is part of the problem. Researchers, police, schools, and tech platforms all use the term NVE, but they don’t always mean the same thing. Here is where they appear to agree versus where they don’t.

Where Experts Agree

Hatred of humanity in general. A recent review of NVE definitions found that most share a small set of core elements (Zdjelar, 2026), and misanthropy leads the list. Unlike prejudice aimed at a specific group, misanthropy is hatred of people in general. The group No Lives Matter calls ordinary people “mundane” and urges members to spread “terror to all who are mundane.” One recruiter put out a call for “true misanthropic individuals” (Njohsp).

Status earned through harm. The second widely shared feature is clout-chasing: gaining attention and rank by committing cruelty, or coercing others to do so. Leaked chat archives from 764, one of the most notorious NVE networks, show a hierarchy in which members climb by producing violent content (Argentino, 2025). Victims, often young girls, are groomed, pressured into sending explicit images, and then extorted into harming themselves on camera. That footage is collected in “lorebooks” that circulate through the network to control victims and raise the status of perpetrators (Hwang, 2026). The harm is the content, and the content is the currency.

Young people recruiting young people. NVE participants are overwhelmingly young, and so are their victims. Across Com-linked arrests worldwide, the median offender is 19, and the median victim is 13 (Argentino and Lindsay, 2026). Recruitment happens on the platforms where teenagers already spend their time.

Where Experts Disagree

Is there an ideology? The word “nihilistic” suggests these groups believe in nothing, and some researchers agree, describing NVE as violence without a clear ideological motive (ISD, 2025). Others argue that nihilism has become an ideology of its own, with rules and justifications for violence (Gill, 2025). Still others see a “salad bar” of borrowed imagery, such as Nazi symbols, Satanism, and school-shooter fandom, used for shock value rather than belief (Argentino and Lindsay, 2026; Sivignon, 2026). The evidence cuts both ways. A study of 29 adjudicated Com-network cases found that genuine ideological motives did appear in some pathways to offline violence, but often only after violent tendencies were already present (Clemmow and colleagues, 2026).

Is the violence a means to an end? The FBI’s definition says NVEs seek to bring about society’s collapse. Some groups at the edge of this ecosystem fit that description. The Order of Nine Angles (O9A), a satanic neo-Nazi movement, promotes ritual “culling” of people it deems worthless as a path to societal breakdown (Gartenstein-Ross, 2025). Other researchers argue that most NVE actors have no strategic goal and that chaos is the point (Argentino and Lindsay, 2026). Whether groups like O9A fall under the NVE umbrella, or are better understood as accelerationists, is debatable.

Is copycatting a defining feature? Many NVE attackers idolize earlier killers. PERIL found documented veneration of past attackers, most often in online tribute posts, in 62 percent of NVE plots and attacks. Columbine alone was cited in 88 cases across 20 countries (Jensen, 2026). In some online dark fandoms, mass shooters are called “saints.” Yet sextortion networks like the one implicated in Germany may never reference a past attack. Is veneration a core of NVE, or the signature of one branch of it?

Where does NVE end and something else begin? NVE overlaps with a crowd of related labels: the True Crime Community, sadistic online exploitation, participatory memetic violent extremism, and “mixed, unclear, and unstable” ideologies, to name a few. Some researchers treat these as parts of a single NVE ecosystem. Others see distinct problems that call for distinct responses.

Why the Definition Matters Now

Debating definitions can sound like academic hair-splitting. It isn’t. A school counselor, a prosecutor, and a content moderator can look at the same teenager and see three different problems: a mental health crisis, a criminal, a terms-of-service violation. Define the threat too narrowly, and we miss the warning signs. Define it too broadly, and the label sweeps in kids who need help, not handcuffs. Many of the young people involved are both victims and perpetrators.

NVEs pose a rapidly growing and increasingly alarming threat to youth worldwide. Despite the groups’ definitional ambiguity, experts largely agree that misanthropy and clout-chasing sit at the core of nihilistic violent extremism. Other definitional elements are still being debated. Experts should work toward definitional agreement and do so quickly. After all, a threat left undefined is a threat left unchecked.

Co-author Avery Ellis is a psychology student at Louisiana State University.

item.title: Why "Face-to-Face Only" Might Be Costing You Good Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

Why "Face-to-Face Only" Might Be Costing You Good Therapy

A former telehealth skeptic on why “in-person only” might be costing you.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Many clinicians, me included, saw telehealth as a stopgap. The results said otherwise.
  • Face-to-face matters, but "in-person only" as a blanket rule is black-and-white thinking.
  • Telehealth isn’t right for everyone. Options are worth discussing with your therapist.
Source: Pexels/Karola G

I’ve been noticing a trend, a shift, across psychology and therapy platforms. It’s the “only face-to-face” request. “In person only,” “No telehealth,” from referral requests to consumers, I see it everywhere.

Look, I get it. I truly get it. Prior to COVID, I swore I would never do telehealth. Only in rare cases, where it was the only way someone would get support, would I even consider it.

So, understandably, the start of COVID was not an easy transition for me. Lockdowns meant that those rare cases where I would consider it now applied to everyone, and people needed support more than ever. So, like many of my colleagues, I did the training, dived deep on what was possible, and did the best I could. And what I found were... results. It was not the terrible outcome I had anticipated, but more than that, it was not just something to hold the fort until I could get back to ‘real therapy’. It worked.

So, post-COVID, I started doing more, until now, full disclaimer: I run a telehealth-only practice, so it’s fair to say I may hold some bias in this space.

I also get why the pendulum has swung. Post-COVID, we're living in a world where a lot of us are lacking face-to-face connections. We spent years on screens, we worked on screens, we saw our families on screens, our kids went to school on screens, we threw our birthday parties on, yup, screens. So it makes sense that we've come out the other side and decided, maybe rightly so, that online interactions just aren't as good. Here’s this thing, I back this, we absolutely do need face-to-face interactions. But this is where we get stuck in black-and-white thinking. Online bad; in-person good. Rather than leveraging screen time to buy us more face-to-face in the spaces that matter most.

But you folks know me, let’s check what the evidence actually says about it all.

What the evidence actually says

Telehealth therapy has actually been shown to be as effective as face-to-face therapy. A 2021 meta-analysis comparing live video therapy with in-person therapy found that therapy is no less effective when it's delivered by video, with the strongest results for CBT for depression and anxiety. The authors concluded that video therapy isn't just the convenient choice, it's one now backed by evidence. A 2025 meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in children, adolescents and their parents found the same thing. Video therapy was as effective as in-person treatment, both straight after treatment and at follow-up.

This was seen in couples' work too. A study of over 1,100 married clients in couple therapy found teletherapy was as effective as in-person therapy for outcomes including relationship satisfaction, sexual satisfaction and the therapeutic alliance.

The big worry I hear, from clinicians especially, is about the therapeutic relationship. Can you really connect through a screen? It's a fair question, and the honest answer from what I have found is that the alliance holds up well. A review of studies on this found a good working alliance and good outcomes across all of them, and outcomes that were equivalent to face-to-face. Now, the alliance scores sat a touch lower on average, and the research isn't conclusive yet that they're fully equal. But the outcomes held up.

Telehealth could potentially give us more face-to-face, not less

This is the big bit I think we're missing. If what we're craving is more in-person connection, telehealth might actually be part of how we get it. It potentially allows us more time to engage in person in the situations that are more meaningful.

We can fit our therapy around our work and our lives, and save that important face-to-face time for family, friends, and community. The hour you'd have spent driving across town, finding parking, sitting in a waiting room and driving home again? That could be dinner with your kids. A walk with a friend. Actually turning up to the thing you keep saying you'll go to. This is no way going to be the case for everyone, but again, if we get stuck in that black-and-white thinking that one is superior to the other, then those who would actually benefit end up missing out.

And when it comes to sex therapy...

The other thing to consider, particularly when we look at sex therapy, is that there's some emerging evidence it might actually be easier for us to talk about things like sex, and those topics that feel vulnerable and exposing, when we have this perceived barrier or distance between us.

Psychologist John Suler described this back in 2004 as the online disinhibition effect: some people self-disclose more often, or more intensely, online than they would in person. We usually talk about the toxic side of that, the trolls and the pile-ons. But Suler also described the flip side, where people share more openly and ask for help more freely.

We see a version of this in sexual health research, too. Studies comparing computer-based questionnaires with face-to-face interviews consistently find people report more sensitive sexual behaviours when there's a screen rather than a person in front of them. In one survey from the Cleveland Clinic, 44% of men said they'd prefer to talk to their doctor about sexual health problems online or by phone because they were too embarrassed to do it face-to-face.

Back to COVID, when sexologists in Portugal were surveyed about moving their work online during lockdown, many reported that their clients felt less exposed, with fewer psychological and emotional barriers to get past. So being at home could ease some of the tension about opening up and remove some of the barriers when it comes to getting help for sexual issues. Some also said it made it easier for clients to talk about gender and sexual orientation, with less stigma. That tracks with what I see in my day-to-day too.

Let’s reframe the "one is better "idea

Absolute disclaimer: None of this means telehealth is right for everyone, or every time. Some people don't have a private space at home. Some couples find it hard to get uninterrupted time together without kids. Some people need the ritual of leaving the house and going somewhere. And yes, sometimes that disinhibition means people share a lot, quickly, and, as therapists, we need to pace that with care.

But "face-to-face only" as a blanket rule? That's the black-and-white thinking I’m not so sure about. It might be ruling out a therapist who's exactly right for you. It might be ruling out the very format that would make it easier to say the hard thing. Like most things when it comes to psychology, I suggest we move into a space of curiosity rather than good/bad and make a choice that fits best for individual needs.

item.title: 5 Evidence-Based Treatments for Borderline Personality Disorder
item.description:
Borderline Personality Disorder

5 Evidence-Based Treatments for Borderline Personality Disorder

How therapy selection shapes outcome and recovery.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • BPD is treatable, with several evidence-based approaches that can help people make meaningful improvements.
  • DBT, MBT, TFP, and GPM focus on different aspects of BPD, yet none consistently outperforms the others.
  • Newer treatments like BPD Compass aim to make care more personalized, efficient, and accessible.

For a long time, borderline personality disorder (BPD) was considered one of the most difficult mental health conditions to treat. Some therapists even believed that people with BPD couldn't get better.

Fortunately, decades of research have demonstrated otherwise. Today, several treatments can help people with BPD manage intense emotions, build healthier relationships, and reduce impulsive behaviors.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) is probably the best known, but it's not the only option. Here are five approaches worth considering if you're looking for care for yourself or a loved one.

1. Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT)

Developed by psychologist Marsha Linehan, DBT was the first treatment for BPD to demonstrate effectiveness in a randomized clinical trial.

The results were incredibly promising. Among chronically suicidal women with BPD, those receiving DBT engaged in less self-harm, had fewer psychiatric hospitalizations, and were more likely to stay in treatment than those receiving usual care.

Since then, DBT has been evaluated in dozens of randomized clinical trials. Its strongest evidence is for reducing suicidal and self-injurious behaviors, although promising findings extend to substance use, eating disorders, and depression.

DBT is based on the idea that people with BPD experience emotions intensely and may rely on coping strategies that provide temporary relief but create problems in the long run.

According to the treatment manual, comprehensive (full model) DBT programs include several components: weekly individual therapy, weekly skills group, and between-session phone coaching. In individual therapy, it is common to review difficulties that came up during the week and explore alternative responses. In skills group, patients receive didactic (class-like) instruction in four skill areas: mindfulness, emotion regulation, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness. Between-session phone coaching helps people apply these skills when they need them most.

Initially, Marsha Linehan recommended that people with BPD make a year-long commitment to their DBT program. However, many DBT programs now offer care for shorter durations (e.g., 6 months).

2. Mentalization-Based Treatment (MBT)

Developed by psychologist Peter Fonagy and psychiatrist Anthony Bateman, MBT has demonstrated improvements in BPD symptoms, self-harm, and interpersonal functioning in randomized clinical trials.

MBT focuses on improving mentalizing, our ability to understand our own thoughts and feelings and those of others. Rather than explicitly teaching coping skills, as in DBT, therapists help patients strengthen this ability through interactions during therapy.

For example, imagine leaving a session convinced your therapist was annoyed with you. Rather than simply reassuring you, an MBT therapist might explore what happened and what each of you might have been thinking or feeling.

The therapeutic relationship becomes a place to practice navigating emotionally charged interactions. Treatment typically includes weekly individual and group sessions over 12–18 months.

3. Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (TFP)

Developed by psychiatrist Otto Kernberg and colleagues, TFP has demonstrated improvements in BPD symptoms and interpersonal functioning in randomized clinical trials.

Like MBT, TFP focuses on relationships rather than teaching specific coping skills. However, TFP emphasizes difficulties integrating positive and negative perceptions of ourselves and others.

For example, someone with BPD might see their partner as loving and trustworthy one moment, but cruel and uncaring after a disagreement. TFP helps patients recognize that positive and negative qualities can exist in the same person.

Treatment typically involves twice-weekly individual sessions lasting a year or longer.

4. Good Psychiatric Management (GPM)

Developed by psychiatrist John Gunderson, GPM takes a different approach; the goal is to make effective BPD treatment accessible through generalist mental health clinicians.

Rather than requiring extensive training in specialized psychotherapy, GPM provides a practical framework for understanding BPD, managing crises, and improving everyday functioning.

Particular attention is given to relationships, work, school, and other meaningful activities. Treatment typically involves weekly appointments, with flexibility based on patients' needs.

Importantly, a randomized clinical trial comparing general psychiatric management with DBT found substantial improvements in both groups, including reductions in suicidal and self-injurious behaviors.

This work challenged the assumption that effective BPD treatment necessarily requires a highly specialized, intensive program.

5. BPD Compass

BPD Compass is a newer cognitive-behavioral treatment my colleagues and I developed to make evidence-based BPD care more efficient and accessible.

We were intrigued that existing treatments all produce meaningful improvements, with no single approach consistently outperforming the others. This suggests that each addresses something important, whether that's emotion regulation (DBT), relationships (MBT, TFP), or building a meaningful life (GPM).

Yet many patients continue experiencing symptoms after treatment. We wondered whether nonresponse might reflect a mismatch between patients' difficulties and the treatment they receive.

We designed BPD Compass to address three broad vulnerabilities associated with BPD: emotion dysregulation, relationship difficulties, and impulsivity. In our clinical trials, treatment begins with an assessment to identify which patterns are driving a particular patient's symptoms, followed by an individualized plan emphasizing the most relevant modules.

BPD Compass takes 18 sessions, considerably shorter than many established BPD treatments. Like GPM, it was designed for generalist clinicians without requiring extensive specialized training.

In an initial randomized clinical trial, participants receiving BPD Compass showed large improvements in BPD symptoms. Subsequent research also documented improvements in emotional, relational, and impulsive functioning, as well as symptoms of co-occurring conditions.

Which Treatment Is Right for Me?

BPD is an incredibly heterogeneous condition. Some people experience frequent suicidal crises and need intensive, long-term support. Others may make meaningful progress with a shorter intervention.

As a BPD treatment developer, my goal isn't to replace existing treatments. It's to expand the options available. Not everyone with BPD needs year-long therapy, and we should have effective, personalized alternatives for those who don't.

Ultimately, the best treatment is one that addresses your difficulties, provides the support you need, and is accessible enough for you to receive it.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Is Your Obsession Actually Limerence?
item.description:
Limerence

Is Your Obsession Actually Limerence?

The specific features of limerence reveal why it can be so problematic.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Limerence is an intense one-sided attachment marked by uncertainty and rumination.
  • The cognitive and emotional components of limerence often occur within a context where someone seeks intimacy.
  • Limerence has been conceptualized to develop over a series of stages.
  • Scholars are only beginning to understand this complex manifestation of the attachment system.

The experience and expression of human attachment is complex, to say the least. As humans, we may share a universal ingrained wiring for connection, but how we navigate this interpersonal world is not the same from person to person.

Are you someone who obsesses about others? Maybe you understand infatuation in the early stages of love, but then know how to transition to a mutual relationship or let go? Forming steady and stable connections is easy for some people; others are tortured with intense and uncertain attachments. New research provides insight into limerence, a specific form of intense attachment that is starting to gain more attention.

What Is Limerence?

Imagine someone fixating on another person. This isn't hard to do. We hear about it on podcasts, watch it unfold in fantastic crime dramas, and, of course, some of us experience it in real life. From infatuation to unrequited love, examples of preoccupations with another person, outside of established relationships, color the romantic landscape. Limerence, however, is different.

Limerence is an intense and highly disruptive cognitive and emotional experience (Marshall et al., 2025; Tennov, 1979). Individuals in the throes of limerence are overwhelmed by the desire to be viewed positively by a specific someone else (i.e., the limerence object). This obsession manifests as uncontrollable rumination to the point that it interferes with day-to-day life.

How Limerence Works

Limerence is typically expressed toward someone with whom the experiencer is highly unlikely to form a real relationship. On the surface, this might seem like unrequited love, but it is far more intense and generally less realistic.

From a case study analysis, Wyant (2021) offered the following pathway by which people might come to experience limerence:

  1. Foundation. The person has low self-worth.
  2. Context. The person holds real-life relationship assumptions that interfere with forming intimate relationships (e.g., people can't handle me; no one can fulfill my emotional needs), or they carry a strong uncertainty (possibly unacknowledged) about whether they should persist in their current relationship.
  3. Strategy. The person copes by seeking positive regard from someone with whom it is unrealistic that they would actually form a relationship (i.e., the limerence object). They become highly sensitive to signs of their approval or disapproval.
  4. Cognitive Fixation. The person comes to idealize their limerence object, thinking they are perfect and wishing they had their life. Rumination and imagination strengthen the fixation.
  5. Emotional Anchoring. The person feels an array of moving emotions, from anxiety and guilt to extremely positive emotions after a positive interaction with the person, to self-loathing. The body can physically react to the thoughts and emotions tied to experiencing limerence.
  6. Rituals. People experiencing limerence imagine their limerence object and ruminate about their object; they are anxious to connect with their object and experience their approval. Uncertainty encourages intensity in this desire for approval, which can feel like the only way they will feel better (i.e., less anxious).

How Does Limerence Develop Over Time?

A recent review (Bradbury et al., 2025) summarized a step-wise sequence proposed by Verhulst (1984). This model suggests that limerence begins in the context of need: a person's needs for emotional intimacy, support, and connection are not fulfilled in their current relationships. Limerence can follow from there:

  1. Stage 1: A person deeply desires to be loved, but is not having this need fulfilled. This setting provides the opportunity for limerence.
  2. Stage 2: A target is identified (a limerence object), often such that they are safe and unattainable. The limerence experiencer feels connection. When there is no direct rejection, the limerence experiencer deepens their (unilateral) attachment to their limerence object.
  3. Stage 3: Ongoing interactions with the limerence object can leave a person uncertain and on an emotional rollercoaster that rides the wave of perceived approval or disapproval of the limerence object. Ruminating and intense sensitivity to the limerence object's reactions persist. Any interaction with the limerence object evokes a strong cognitive and emotional response.
  4. Stage 4: The limerence dissolves over time. Desires for reconnection can spike, and anxiety and guilt may characterize this stage.
  5. Stage 5: The limerence no longer persists, and the possibility exists for a healthier relationship with the former limerence object. The intensity of the earlier stages can make a new relationship difficult, but it is possible.

Limerence and Other Psychological Constructs

Different dimensions of limerence are predictable by key psychological constructs. Recent research suggests limerence is best understood as a two-dimensional construct, comprised of both an intense need for attachment and neglect of self or others (Marshall et al., 2025).

Attachment anxiety, imaginative fantasy (i.e., the tendency to daydream), and the need to belong are linked to the need-for-attachment dimension of limerence for those experiencing it. This dimension is also predicted by psychological inflexibility and emotional dependence, obsessive preoccupation, self-conscious anxiety, and idealization (Marshall et al., 2025). The neglect dimension operates similarly, except it is not predicted by attachment orientation or idealization, and is associated with more social anxiety and lower self-esteem.

There's More to Learn About Limerence

Whereas scholars have noted parallels between limerence and addiction and noted the potential path from limerence to stalking (e.g., Bradbury et al., 2025), there's reason to suggest that limerence can also serve as a coping mechanism in an unfulfilling relational context. Experiencing limerence can be a one-time experience or repeated, short-lived or long (Tennov, 1979), yet the context in which it occurs offers the suggestion that it is the mind's way of addressing an undermet need for belonging and intimacy. The field has much more to learn about limerence as an unusual manifestation of the human attachment system.

item.title: Why You May Need an "Elevator Message" About Healthy Aging
item.description:
Bias

Why You May Need an "Elevator Message" About Healthy Aging

Thoughtless ageist comments can affect children, young adults, and you.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Negative and false beliefs about aging can affect the longterm health of young people.
  • Positive beliefs about aging correlate with 7.5 more years of life and better health, according to research.
  • Create "elevator messages" to educate children and young people about the benefits of getting older.

“Of all the self-fulfilling prophecies in our culture the assumption that aging means decline and poor health is probably the deadliest.” --Marilyn Ferguson, author

Source: Image by Pickpic.

An Awkward Situation on an Elevator

I was in an elevator with two preschool children in Halloween costumes, their parents, and an older couple.

The older man commented to the smiling children, “Oh, you are going to have fun on Halloween, I see.” The children and parents nodded at him in the affirmative.

Then he sighed and said, “When you’re my age, you have a lot of aches and pains. Life is not as much fun when you get older.”

I was taken aback. So many negative stereotypes about aging in two short sentences, including the classic myth that old age is an inevitable process of decline and deterioration. I responded, “I don’t agree. I’m 82, and I’m enjoying life more than ever.”

The man said, “Well, I’m 73. You look very young for your age.” Was he implying that I was the exception that proved the rule?

I’m not above fishing for compliments, but in this case, I was after something more important—sending positive messages about aging to young children. I never realized I was going to need an “elevator message” to do it.

The Elevator Message

Usually, an “elevator message” refers to a business networking tool, consisting of one or two short sentences about who you are, what you do, and how your skills could benefit the listener, according to speaking coach Fred Miller. The idea of an elevator message is to convey the most important things about you during a short elevator ride. "Elevator messages" don't need to take place in actual elevators, of course. These messages can be employed at conferences, book signings, or even in the line at the coffee house. Writers, for example, can describe their background and latest book project; job-seekers can tout their most important accomplishments.

I had never previously considered that I might someday need an elevator message to combat stereotypes about aging. What I said was simply a gut reaction to the situation. And the reason I am still mulling over what I said, and what I could have said, is because there was a life-and-death situation at stake. Well, not exactly, but here’s the research.

The Vital Importance of a Positive View About Aging

Psychology professor Becca Levy has researched the health and longevity effects of age beliefs. In one study, published in 2002, she and her colleagues followed 660 adults 50 and older and discovered that participants with a positive view of aging lived on average 7.5 years longer than participants with a negative view of aging.

In her 2022 book, Breaking the Age Code, Levy cites other studies showing that people who held positive age beliefs scored 30% better on memory tests than those with negative age beliefs. She has also discovered that age stereotypes affect a surprising number of areas—for example, those with negative age beliefs had a slower gait, lower self-esteem, and exercised less. (For more details, check out this blog on how positive age beliefs can reduce dementia risk.)

Add to these results the amazing finding that most older people are happier people, as shown by numerous surveys. I was so shocked to learn the relationship between aging and happiness that I wrote a whole book (Silver Sparks) and numerous blogs about it. In addition, older people have good mental health, including a positive outlook on life. As researcher Laura Carstensen states: “People over the age of 65 have the most stable and optimistic outlook of all adults.”

Of course, one negative comment in an elevator would be unlikely to mold the mentality of those young children. But I would suspect that a drumbeat of negative, ageist comments like the one I overheard could eventually have an effect on the mental outlook of those who hear them…which is everybody.

Young children and young adults are not the only ones who could benefit from an age-positive elevator message. A thoughtful message might also remind older people to challenge their own internalized ageism and recall the benefits of getting older.

Better Elevator Messages

Can we construct pithy elevator messages to replace the knee-jerk comments about ageism?

To jog your brain, consider these elevator messages about aging that are positive and accurate:

  • “Getting older is fun because you have more choices about how to spend your time.”
  • “Getting older gives you more time for hobbies like painting, dancing, gardening, photography, and writing.”
  • “When you are older, you can travel to places you’ve dreamed of seeing all your life.”
  • “Older people can spend more time with friends and family.”
  • “Older people are happier people because they have more time to do the things they’ve always wanted to do.”
  • “Older people don’t let little things bother them; they've learned to enjoy life more.”

What we say to children about aging will, of course, depend upon the age of the child and the situation.

With better messages about aging, we can help children face their future with optimism, possibly affecting their lifespan, healthspan, and mental health. And by voicing the positive truths about aging, we could also remind ourselves of the many advantages of growing older.

Here’s a challenge for you: What’s your idea for an elevator message about the benefits of growing older?

item.title: Does Banning Phones in School Boost Test Scores?
item.description:
Education

Does Banning Phones in School Boost Test Scores?

Are we asking the right questions? Thinking happens when a child gets stuck.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • One large study found modest academic gains in schools with strict, all-day phone bans.
  • Repeatedly resisting the urge to check a phone may consume attention needed for learning.
  • Reading comprehension depends on recognizing misunderstandings and taking time to repair them.
  • Removing phones from classrooms may give students more opportunities to persist through difficult tasks.

You might know a child who can read every word in a paragraph but still not know what it means. Maybe she misunderstood why a character left their home, or why two people were talking in a certain conversation. She might keep reading until she stops understanding and realizes that she does. She might go back to find what she’s done wrong, or she might keep going. At the end of the page, she might have no idea what she’d actually read.

We may focus on test scores and forget the need to wrestle with questions.
Source: Pexels/Ron Lach

In my work as a speech pathologist, I’ve studied that type of breakdown for many years. When readers notice their mistakes, they might return to the earlier pages or rethink what they initially thought. But they have to hold the earlier information in mind. They have to have gaps where they can start to think about it and process. Those gaps take sustained attention and time. I’ve written about what happens in those gaps as productive uncertainty, the quality of sitting with and wrestling with questions.

I was thinking about those gaps in the context of two large studies on school phone bans that were released this year. The studies examined whether students score higher on tests when they have no phones available. One study suggested that they do, but only by a small margin. The other suggested that the scores hardly improve.

While this data are important, I’m more interested in how the process of learning shifts when students are less interrupted by phones. A phone within reach asks a child to keep deciding not to look at it, and each of these decisions draws on the attention she needs for the page.

Locking Phones Away Removes Repeated Distractions

A recent study by Thomas Kane and colleagues at the Harvard Center for Education Policy Research was revealing. They found schools that locked phones away during the day saw small gains in test scores compared with similar schools that did not.

In the Harvard Gazette, Kane pointed out that teachers differ in how much they enforced no-phone rules, and that with a strict ban, “you’re not relying on teachers to enforce it.” That may suggest an environmental reason. Imagine a student who has a phone in their pocket, and the teacher sometimes forgets or doesn’t want to argue. The child might check a message or think about checking a message and decide not to. But then their phone might ring or beep, and the same decision comes up again. Each time, the child’s attention leaves the paragraph they were trying to understand.

But when the environmental conditions are changed, that is when the phones are completely locked away, the rule no longer depends on each teacher's vigilance. This also removes the need to make the phones a battleground, as in many classrooms it will inevitably become that.

I recently came across a comment by David Figlio, an economist at the University of Rochester. As he told NPR, at 55, he still has to resist looking at a text when his phone buzzes in his pocket. “Now imagine you’re a 14-year-old.” This comment strikes me as well-put because it shows how much we’re asking of children when we expect them to somehow stand up to addictive technologies. We treat it as a question of will and morality, even though companies designed these phones to be as addictive as possible.

Distractions Interrupt Reflection

Changing your environment matters because learning takes sustained attention. As in the initial example, when a child loses their place on the page or misinterprets a sentence, sustained attention helps them backtrack and self-correct. She might have a chance to reflect on what went wrong and understand what she needs to do next.

Even without AI, if students have access to a phone, the simple distraction of looking at it or thinking to look at it can interrupt those moments of reflection. They might look up an answer to a comprehension question, without realizing the need to go back and reread the text. This is a very minor slip in the moment, but if you repeat these day in and day out, the changes in what’s being learned and what’s only being written down add up.

The same goes for adults. Productive uncertainty is easy to ignore or push aside, especially if we have ready answers. In addition, it can feel as if we’re being more efficient when we do so. That sense of efficiency can compound and make us more interested in getting the answers faster. Especially since we have no school bans for ourselves, we might find ourselves simply glancing at our phones in moments of difficult thought. Say we’re stuck on how to phrase a hard email, or unsure what we think about a decision. The pull to check the phone tends to arrive right at that moment of difficulty, which is also the moment when the thinking would have happened. We get an answer, but we have lost the chance to think for ourselves.

That’s why the environmental conditions matter far more than we think. Willpower is one thing, but the cognitive drain of needing that willpower all the time can make it harder to have deeper or more sustained thoughts.

The next time someone asks you to focus harder, or asks a child to, ask them what conditions are making it more difficult. Make one change, and then reassess. You might find that it has far less to do with willpower than you thought.

item.title: The Music of Thanksgiving: Thirty Voices at One Table
item.description:
Gratitude

The Music of Thanksgiving: Thirty Voices at One Table

Family and friends singing builds connection and communal gratitude.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Shared singing across ages 3 to 76 synchronizes breathing and heart rates while building connection.
  • Inviting song requests shifts gatherings from passive listening to active participation.
  • Group singing supports physiological alignment, turning holiday ritual into shared resonance.
  • Shared singing turns a busy holiday meal into a communal ritual making gratitude, visible across generations.
Singing Grandmothers
Source: AI-Generated Image

Thanksgiving as a musical holiday? What possibilities!

Christmas has its carols and the Fourth of July its rousing bands. Thanksgiving is usually defined by motion and aroma, the joyful hum of conversation, the clatter of silverware (or plasticware), the scent of favorite holiday family foods, perhaps the sound of bickering siblings (both young and adult), and the sigh of aahs when the turkey finally emerges from the oven.

This year our gathering will have a new sound: two grandmothers leading the family in song.

We’re bringing together two extended families, about thirty people under one roof. The youngest is three years old; the oldest is seventy-six. Many ages, memories, opinions, football fans, and personalities are all under one roof. After dinner, or perhaps before everyone hits the food sleepies, we’ll sing “Over the River and Through the Wood,” followed by “You Are My Sunshine.”

Some will know every word. Others may remember only the chorus. The youngest may sing a few words, hum, add their own sounds, or even bang out the beat with a wooden spoon. What fun as the elders turn down their hearing aids. Someone may come in early; someone else may be a beat behind. And of course, good old Uncle, who we won’t name, can’t carry a tune. This is not a choir that has rehearsed together, although Ethan and Sara will help guide us. We’re gathering as a family, not auditioning for a TV talent show.

“Over the River and Through the Wood”

The two songs we chose to begin carry different kinds of familiarity. “Over the River and Through the Wood” belongs to the season, with its image of traveling to a family gathering. “You Are My Sunshine” is a song many people have known since childhood, although the version one person remembers may not be quite the version another learned. We may have to help each other with a word or two, and someone may remember a verse the rest of us have forgotten.

The song sheet is a simple idea, but we like the question at the bottom. “What else should we sing?” might bring up a song someone’s parent used to sing, a tune from a school play, or something the children are listening to now. A suggestion may come with a story the family has heard many times before, but still loves to hear. Sometimes a song is a favorite because it’s funny, easy to sing, or simply familiar.

Thanksgiving Songsheet
Source: Mozart for Munchkins/Used with permission

The toddler might not know all the words, and the teenagers might roll their eyes before joining in, increasing the volume of the room. Someone might begin to think about doing the dishes, but for a few brief moments, we might have the gift of nobody checking a phone — just the collective shared wave of sound and rhythm.

Groove

Singing together can help coordinate our breathing and even influence patterns in our heart rates. But you don't need to measure any of that to notice what happens when people sing together. We listen to one another, adjust our voices, and try to stay with the group.

A large family gathering doesn’t often ask everyone to do the same thing at once. In smaller Thanksgiving gatherings, we’ve gone around the table asking questions like, “What are you grateful for" and "What have you done to help someone else feel grateful?" We use a homemade placemat asking about gratitude.

People catch up in small groups. The children move in and out of the room. Someone is tending to the food while someone else clears a place at the table. Singing gives us a few minutes with one shared activity.

Conducting the Day Together

Hopefully, a song sheet encourages all voices and squeals to join in. Inviting family members to suggest a favorite tune shifts the dynamic to active participation and gives everyone a voice. When you ask people what they want to sing, you are really asking: What memory do you bring to this table? What tune makes you feel at home?

The songs aren’t performance, just connection. We know that someone may have to retrieve a wandering toddler or may pause while a plate is passed or a child asks for something from the kitchen. The music may stop and start. In a gathering of thirty people, a perfectly uninterrupted performance seems unlikely.

Afterward, we’ll return to the conversations already underway, half of us forgetting what we were talking about anyway. People will share dessert, tell stories, and catch up with relatives they don’t see every week. Later, when the house is quieter, there may be time for a longer conversation or a cup of coffee. Those parts of the day matter, too.

Gratitude as a Collective Chord

Thanksgiving Placemat
Source: Mozart for Munchkins/Used with permission

Gratitude is often a quiet reflection, perhaps first thing in the morning, or quietly before falling asleep. Thanksgiving is a social ritual, giving us the chance to make our gratitude visible and communal.

Long before the final slice of pie is served, a shared song reminds us why we gathered in the first place. Sure, we'll also eat too much, complain about how stuffed we are, and probably fall asleep earlier than planned.

Keeping the Chord Alive

As the holiday draws to a close and the house settles down, the music we made may linger in memory. Maybe during the car rides home, someone hums “You Are My Sunshine.”

When the final chord fades, what remains is the warmth of the ensemble, how it made us feel, collectively, and tunes we will hold on to for next year.

item.title: When They Won’t (or Can’t) Connect: A Musician’s Notes on Listening
item.description:
Education

When They Won’t (or Can’t) Connect: A Musician’s Notes on Listening

How well we respond to disconnection can have huge implications.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • How well we listen to distinguish the reason behind the disconnect will help us let go and move on.
  • Listen for what is missing in a conversation, musical or verbal.
  • Neutralizing our projections helps us connect and helps the other side feel less defensive.
  • Whether we connect with the other person or not, in the process of reaching out, we connect with ourselves.

A few days ago, I attended a talk at Yale’s Jackson School of Global Affairs at the annual Yale Assembly for alumni delegates. When I asked what the most pressing global problems are at the moment, the surprise that caught my ear was “the collapse of the recognition of facts.” When others cherry-pick data that serves their own agenda, it blocks connection. How well we respond to disconnection can have huge implications.

On a Personal Level

Sometimes it’s hard to know if people don’t want to connect, don’t know how, or both. At a class dinner out, the unexpected topic of parents came up. One parent seemed to find pleasure in music more than in her child. Another parent often said to his young daughter, who could not possibly read his adult mind, “You know what I mean, right?” Someone else repeatedly said, “You don’t know what it was like,” and yet could not answer his daughter’s questions about what his traumas were actually like.

Distinguishing “won’t connect” from “can’t connect” would help us understand the context of the disconnect, and that clarity helps us move forward.

As a Freelance Musician

Music is about connection, but musicians are not all naturally gifted at it. However, to stay afloat in the unsupported, wild west of the music industry, we have to upgrade our communication skills like everyone else. We have to connect with our audiences, supporters, partners, and presenters, even when the other side doesn’t want to – or doesn’t know how to – connect back.

My work in music is often misunderstood to be the work of playing notes quickly and accurately. But it is the moment-to-moment listening and the consequent response that create the spirit of the piece, not the individual notes. This year I am taking my piano studio to perform in Rome, to practice performing as responding to a new environment in the moment.

Most of my time is spent listening for what is still missing. Building connections between the different musical elements helps me to infer the composer’s intent. In conversation too, creating a tensegrity of multidimensional motivations helps me to tease out what the speaker is not saying, before I make any interpretations.

Bring A Willingness to Play

Author Iain McGilchrist posits that the search for truth requires four avenues of inquiry: science, reason, intuition, and imagination. We have to play with our awareness of not just the past and present, but the future. Only with whole-brain processing (both left and right sides) can we approach the complexity of truth.

Well-meaning people with a trust deficit may regress to hearing only their inner bubble of a few familiar themes and pre-formulated responses. We can challenge that response by labeling it, for example, “It seems like you are angry about this.” Even a wrong guess works, because they will have the urge to correct it, and that reveals something. If we are tolerant enough to wait and listen, we may draw out secrets that will change everything about our connection.

Neutralize Projections

When we anticipate that a conversation or an encounter will not be pleasant, we greatly reduce its chances of building a connection. Our counterpart, when expecting friction, does the same.

FBI negotiator Chris Voss shares a technique he calls “neutralizing negativity.” When we emotionally prepare the other side by saying “you are not going to like this,” you have taken the sting out of the interaction. I tried this with my Yale Alumni College class last week, where we studied two works by Mozart and Bartók. Before I introduced the difficult music of Bartók, I asked them to notice their posture towards their listening, as compared with how they had listened to the Mozart. While both works are intense, Mozart is associated with easy listening and Bartók with unpleasant dissonance. While listening to the unfamiliar dissonance of Bartók still took a lot of effort, the naming of this negative posture effectively helped people connect more than they would have otherwise.

When They Only Want a Transaction From Us

A colleague recently shared that when she volunteered to be a mentor, she discovered her mentees just wanted her contacts and did not want to connect. I don’t know whether to cry or laugh, because in my youth, I would have done anything to find mentors who wanted to connect with me and not just my success.

I do still believe that with a persistent repetition of stating our values, we can build up both our integrity and their awareness for the potential of future connection. We have more power in calling out these moments than most of us realize or act on.

Meanwhile, the above strategies worked for my business negotiations this week. But even if the connection had failed, I am still learning so much from processing these tricky relational crossroads. As Stephen Nachmanovitch writes in his marvelous book Free Play, “Trusting someone else can involve gigantic risks, and it leads to the even more challenging task of learning to trust yourself.” In music and in life, through the process of reaching out, we connect more deeply with ourselves.

item.title: 4 Ways to Support Eating Disorder Recovery This Holiday Season
item.description:
Eating Disorders

4 Ways to Support Eating Disorder Recovery This Holiday Season

How loved ones can help with recovery without adding to holiday stress.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Comments about weight and dieting can make the holidays harder for someone in eating disorder recovery.
  • Avoid making someone's eating disorder the focus of every conversation.
  • Including loved ones in holiday traditions can reduce the isolation that often comes with eating disorders.
Source: Photo by Jarden Bellamkonda on Unsplash

The holidays are about spending time with friends and family, traditions, and meals. For someone in recovery from an eating disorder, though, the changes in routine, new foods, and comments about eating and weight can make what is supposed to be an enjoyable time feel overwhelming.

Even someone who's made considerable progress in their eating disorder recovery can find themselves plagued by eating disorder thoughts or anxious about situations which previously would have been quite manageable. Family can be a source of this stress, especially when the subject of dieting, exercise, and appearance comes up.

In my work as a psychotherapist specializing in eating disorders, I've found that most family members and friends genuinely want to be supportive. But even with the best intentions, they may not realize how their words or actions affect someone in recovery. Here are four ways loved ones can offer support during the holidays.

1. Leave Weight, Dieting, and Food Commentary Out of the Conversation

How many times do you have conversations about food and weight over the holidays? Someone will be saying they're going to skip breakfast so they've got room for dinner. Someone else will be talking about their New Year’s resolution to lose weight. A relative will comment on someone's looks or joke about having to go to the gym after dessert.

These comments are so ubiquitous that we tend to just ignore them. For someone in the eating disorder recovery process, though, those same comments can be a reinforcement of the very beliefs they're trying to dismantle (that certain foods are "bad," that you have to "earn" your food, that your body size is a measure of your worth, etc.). Try to avoid commenting on what other people are eating, how much they're eating, or whether their bodies have changed. This includes compliments about weight loss. You may not know why someone's weight has changed, and what you think is "just being nice" may actually reinforce eating disorder thoughts and behaviors. These comments also contribute to weight bias and stigma.

Pay attention to how you talk about your own eating, too. Describing yourself as "bad" for having dessert, or saying you're going to have to make it up, sends the message that eating is something you should feel guilty about.

If another family member is starting to go down the diet-calories-and-body line of thinking, consider changing the subject. The person in eating disorder recovery doesn't necessarily have to be the one to speak up and set that boundary.

2. Respect Their Meal Plan and Eating Schedule

Holiday meals don't always happen at predictable times. Dinner may be served several hours later than usual, people may skip meals in anticipation of a large gathering, or there may be an expectation that everyone should eat at the same time.

For someone in the recovery phase from an eating disorder, eating regularly throughout the day may be an essential part of the treatment. They may need a snack just before the main holiday meal, or may need to eat when the rest of the family are skipping a meal because they want to leave room for dinner.

Comments like "You'll spoil your appetite" or "Can't you just wait until dinner?" can make an already stressful situation more difficult. What may be a very minor change in plans to someone without an eating disorder may be much more complicated for someone working to establish regular eating patterns.

If you're hosting, consider asking ahead of time whether there's anything you can do to help. You don't need to make an announcement or draw attention to someone's eating. Simply having food available in case they need to eat when others aren't can be helpful.

Unless you're directly involved in supporting your loved one's meal plan as part of their treatment, avoid monitoring their portions or questioning what they're eating. Even when it comes from a place of concern, having someone watch what you eat can increase anxiety and self-consciousness, making eating even more difficult.

3. Remember That They Are More Than Their Eating Disorder

When someone you love has an eating disorder, it's understandable that you might worry about how they're doing. You may wonder whether they're eating enough, how treatment is going, or whether they're struggling more than they're letting on.

When you're together for the holidays, though, try not to let concerns about your loved one's eating disorder dominate your interactions. Eating disorders can take up so much time and mental energy that people may lose interest in activities they once enjoyed, withdraw from relationships, or have difficulty engaging in everyday life. But that doesn't mean every conversation needs to revolve around their eating disorder or how they're doing in treatment.

Talk about things other than food and recovery. Ask about a show they're watching, a book they've read, a movie they've enjoyed, or something else that might interest them. Include them in family conversations and traditions, even if they seem less engaged than they used to be. The idea is to give them opportunities to connect with others without feeling pressured to participate or having every conversation come back to their eating disorder.

4. Don't Expect Them to Be Happy Just Because It's the Holidays

There's a lot of pressure to enjoy the holidays. We're supposed to look forward to family gatherings, appreciate time together, and participate in traditions that are meant to be fun. But the holidays can also bring up anxiety, grief, loneliness, and difficult family dynamics.

For someone in eating disorder recovery, these feelings may be accompanied by anxiety around food and body image or guilt after eating. They may want to be part of the celebration while also feeling desperate to avoid certain aspects of it.

If they say they're having a hard time, you may want to offer reassurance and try to convince them there's nothing to worry about. "It's only one meal," "Just relax," "Don't let that ruin your holiday," etc., are all things people say with the best of intentions but can quite often leave the person feeling misunderstood or frustrated with themselves for having the difficulty they do.

Instead of trying to convince them they shouldn't feel anxious, acknowledge what they're experiencing. You might say, "I know these gatherings can be stressful" or "I'm glad you're here, even though I know this isn't easy." You can also ask whether they'd like some company, want to talk, or need a little space.

Feeling anxious or uncomfortable doesn't necessarily mean someone isn't making progress in their eating disorder recovery. They may be working hard to participate in a holiday meal or eat foods they've previously avoided, even when eating disorder thoughts are especially loud. These experiences can take a lot of effort, and being able to face that discomfort without turning to familiar eating disorder behaviors is an important part of recovery.

A Final Thought

The holidays can be especially challenging for someone with an eating disorder. Being mindful of your words and behaviors, supporting their treatment, and continuing to include them in family traditions can help them feel supported and connected to the people and experiences they care about.

item.title: The Harm of Trying to Change Your Sexual Orientation
item.description:
Sexual Orientation

The Harm of Trying to Change Your Sexual Orientation

Wanting to Change Your Sexual Orientation Doesn’t Make It Harmless

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Self-initiated efforts showed no evidence of changing sexual orientation over two years.
  • People pursuing change reported more depression and less social support.
  • Change efforts were associated with greater concealment and disconnection from oneself.
  • Nearly 63% of those initially pursuing change had stopped by the two-year follow-up.
Source: Image by Pexels from Pixabay

When people hear “conversion therapy,” they may picture a teenager forced into treatment by parents or religious leaders. But efforts to change sexual orientation often begin privately: someone prays for their attractions to disappear, suppresses sexual thoughts, or avoids relationships in hopes of becoming heterosexual.

In March 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that a Colorado ban on conversion therapy may violate free speech rules. Proponents of the ban argued that people who want to change their sexual orientation should be allowed to try. This raises an important question, answered by recent research—what happens when a person sincerely wants this change?

A new study offers a troubling answer: self-initiated efforts to change sexual orientation were associated with greater depression, less social support, and greater disconnection from oneself—without evidence that they changed sexual orientation. Choosing to pursue change does not establish that the pursuit is safe or effective.

Psychologist G. Tyler Lefevor and colleagues followed current and former members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints over two years. Their study included 315 participants with information about change efforts at both assessments. Unlike research that asks people to reconstruct experiences years later, this study followed participants forward in time. The researchers also registered their research plan in advance and assembled a team with differing perspectives on sexual orientation change efforts. This is an important way the researchers demonstrated commitment to objectivity and research ethics.

Nearly three-quarters of participants reported trying to change their same-gender sexuality at some point. Forty-three reported ongoing or recently ended efforts at the beginning of the study.

Those participants were struggling more than people who were no longer trying or had never tried. They reported more depressive symptoms, lower well-being, poorer self-rated health, and less support from friends and family. They were also less open about their sexuality and more alienated from their own experiences.

Two years later, the group initially pursuing change still reported more depression and less support from friends. However, the overall test combining health outcomes was not statistically significant, and the researchers found no significant difference in suicidality. The depression difference averaged about two points on a commonly used questionnaire, with both groups’ averages falling within the mild range.

These findings deserve attention. This was an observational study, and participants were already experiencing distress when it began. It cannot establish whether change efforts caused depression, whether distress encouraged people to pursue change, or whether both reflected other pressures. Most participants were White adults from one religious background, and relatively few were actively pursuing change.

Nevertheless, the findings challenge the reassurance that personally desired change efforts are harmless and should be allowed.

A person can sincerely choose something while carrying painful beliefs about what makes them acceptable. “I want to become straight” may coexist with “I am afraid I will lose my family,” “I cannot imagine belonging in my faith community as I am,” or “My attractions mean there is something wrong with me.”

This study did not establish that these change efforts were entirely free of outside influence. “Self-initiated” describes who undertakes the effort; it does not establish where the desire originated. Nor did it mean everyone worked alone: participants’ experiences could include personal practices, groups, or other assistance.

That distinction matters. An external demand can become an internal rule, enforced without anyone else in the room.

One possible cost is persistent self-surveillance. Every attraction or sexual thought becomes something to monitor. Every unwanted erotic desire or impulse becomes evidence of failure. When attractions persist, a person may conclude that they have not prayed enough, worked hard enough, or shown sufficient commitment.

Another possible cost is isolation. Avoiding people who evoke attraction—or communities that offer acceptance—may reduce opportunities for friendship, intimacy, and honest conversation. The study’s findings of lower support and greater self-alienation fit these concerns, although they do not prove these particular pathways caused the distress.

The promised benefit also failed to materialize in the study’s comparisons. Participants pursuing change showed no significantly different changes in same-gender or other-gender attraction, sexual aversion, or sexual behavior over two years. Nearly 63 percent of those initially classified as pursuing change were no longer doing so by follow-up, having given up trying to change their sexuality.

Sexuality can show natural variation over time. People can also change their behavior, relationships, or identity labels. None of those changes, by itself, demonstrates that an intervention can reliably turn same-gender attraction into heterosexuality.

Respecting personal autonomy remains essential. People deserve to make their own decisions about faith, relationships, sexual behavior, and the language they use for themselves. A therapist should not prescribe a particular identity or relationship.

But respecting someone’s choices also requires being honest about the evidence and helping them examine the costs of their goals. Someone seeking help can explore religious commitments, relationship decisions, grief, and fear without being promised that their attractions can be eliminated. Choosing celibacy or setting boundaries around behavior is a different goal from trying to change the attractions themselves. Sex therapist Jack Morin famously described that when people go to war with their own sexuality, they are likely to end up worse than they started.

The clinical task is to help people build a life they can inhabit with dignity, connection, and less self-rejection.

A sincere desire to become heterosexual does not guarantee that pursuing that goal will help. This research adds to concerns that the pursuit can accompany continuing distress while delivering no demonstrated change in orientation. People experiencing that conflict deserve support that takes both their values and their well-being seriously.

item.title: Why Do I Have to Do Everything?
item.description:
Relationships

Why Do I Have to Do Everything?

The invisible negotiations of intimate relationships.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Every partner contributes to a relationship; rarely is the contribution equal in all domains.
  • Lack of equality can lead to differences in entitlement and power.
  • Instead, relationships should be evaluated as a whole, across all spheres of contribution.
  • Both members must retain autonomy and equality.

Every relationship has its own way of giving and receiving. Partners contribute their money, time, emotional and logistical support, and domestic labor, among other activities and resources. Both give, and both take. But it’s rare that both people contribute equally in all these domains. In other words, in most categories, one person is doing more than the other. Often, one partner ends up feeling angry that they are “doing it all” in the sphere of their focus.

Power Imbalance

Sometimes these differences create a power imbalance. For example, if one person earns significantly more than the other, this can subtly influence how the couple makes a large financial decision. The person who earns less may feel less entitled to their opinions, needs, or wants. They may feel less autonomy. They may also feel an obligation to reciprocate in other ways, even if it’s unspoken. As for the person who contributes more, their role may create a feeling of burden or over-responsibility. This can lead to feelings of resentment or burnout.

Whole System Evaluation

People in intimate relationships may try to rectify or avoid these pitfalls by attempting to make every contribution equal. But given that equal contribution in all spheres is virtually impossible, perhaps avoiding pitfalls needs to entail something other than that. Perhaps the focus needs to be on seeing the system as a whole and evaluating the contribution each makes within it. In other words, one person may earn more, but the other may provide more logistical support or domestic labor. In this way, there may be differences in the spheres of contribution, but as a whole, each partner may feel the arrangement is fair.

Preserving Power and Dignity

Furthermore, it’s crucial that regardless of how much each person contributes, both partners’ decision-making authority, financial independence, and freedom from indebtedness be protected. In other words, just because one partner spends more time on child-rearing, it doesn’t mean the other shouldn’t have an equal say in where that child attends school. And just because one partner earns more money doesn’t mean they should have more authority over how the couple spends it. Of course, the person who carries more responsibility in a particular area may have more expertise or experience, and that deserves consideration. But having more expertise isn’t the same as having more power.

Equality in romantic relationships doesn’t necessarily mean contributing equal amounts of money, time, or labor. It means ensuring that differences in contribution don’t become differences in autonomy, dignity, or power. The goal isn’t to contribute equally to a relationship, but to be aware of all the contributions in all aspects of a shared life. And to recognize that fairness doesn’t necessarily mean equality of contribution. What matters is making sure neither partner’s contribution gives them more ownership of the other person’s life or shared life decisions.

item.title: Why the Word “Boundaries” Makes Boomer Parents Mad
item.description:
Boundaries

Why the Word “Boundaries” Makes Boomer Parents Mad

The tense communication gap between adult daughters and their parents.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Older parents invest more intensely in family ties, while adult children often prioritize independence.
  • Family conflict over boundaries is often about what a decision means more than what it is.
  • Notice that the tension arises because the Boomer parent wants more closeness with her Millennial adult child.
  • Adult daughters and their parents often hear the word “boundaries” in very different ways.

When the topic of boundaries comes up, a Millennial woman (born 1981-1996 according to Pew Research) will vigorously nod in agreement. But when that same daughter tries to install those boundaries with her Baby Boomer mother, (born between 1946-1964, according to Pew Research), the reaction can be swift and negative: Mom gives a raised eyebrow, a long silence, or an extreme and snarky reply.

How did a word meant to build healthier relationships become one that is so triggering? Why do boundaries make your family members feel rejected? The issue isn't the new behavior and delineation itself, but what the word signals.

For some adult daughters (Gen X were born 1965-1980; Millennials born 1981-1996; and even adult Gen Z (born 1997-2012, according to Pew Research), boundaries represent a way to honor yourself, not give up on the elements in a relationship that matter to you, and hopefully reflect your evolving emotional maturity. For a Baby Boomer parent, boundary talk sounds like withdrawal, rejection, and pulling away from the family (or particularly from them).

Boundary Conversations Are Loaded

Part of the problem is that the paradigm of “Boomers vs. Millennials” has become a ready-made cultural storyline. In a 2026 study of Instagram memes about the two generations, media researchers Centorrino and Ferrigno found that the largest group of memes did one thing above all: draw lines between generations. That is, sow division between the Millennial and the Boomer. These memes ranged from dismissive jokes like “OK Boomer” to side-by-side comparisons of what each generation was like at the same age, but with a negative twist. The researchers argue that generational labels work less like neutral categories and more like symbolic boundaries, sorting people into “us” and “them.” It can become a crass classification system or a way of saying "they're not like me and my peers."

With this culturally sensitive division in mind, when a daughter deploys the language of boundaries, her mother may not hear a healthy limit. She may hear one more line being drawn between “your generation” and “mine.” In short, she feels pushed away and made fun of for her behaviors and ways of doing things. That's a pretty big barrier to hearing their adult child in a neutral or healthy way.

Different Life Stages, Different Stakes

Research on adult development helps explain why this mismatch runs so deep. Karen Fingerman, a leading researcher on parents and adult children, and her colleagues draw on socioemotional selectivity theory. This theory suggests that as people age, they become more invested in keeping their longest-standing close ties than in forming new ones. That means they get really zoned-in on their adult children, their own siblings, and lifelong close friends.

In a 2024 study of more than 300 adults aged 65 and older, Fingerman’s team found that nearly three-quarters of participants’ long-term relationships were with family. That means most of what an older person wants is from their adult kids. They're invested in these long-term relationships with a deep intensity. However, the parent-child ties were also complicated. The time older folks spent with their family members was linked to more stressful conversations and intense moods (both positive and negative). All this means that Boomer parents are putting an intense lens on their adult child and it's kind of stressful.

And here's the rub. That intensity only goes one way. Researchers have described the concept of “intergenerational stake”: parents tend to be more invested in their children than children are in their parents. In a 2015 study of more than 600 middle-aged adults, Kira Birditt, Fingerman, and colleagues found that people rated their relationships with their children as both more important and more negative than their relationships with their own parents. Friction, in other words, can be a sign of how much a relationship matters. In sum, the more an adult child matters to their parent, the more likely there's tension as they seek connection.

Why does that friction occur? Fingerman’s earlier work points to an answer. In a 1996 study of 48 mothers over 70 and their middle-aged daughters, she introduced the term “developmental schism” to describe tension that arises because mothers and daughters are at different points in adult development. That's the sandpaper feeling between mothers and adult daughters, even when there's a lot of love. Two of the biggest sources of that tension were independence and how much importance each person places on the relationship. Many of today’s Boomer mothers were once the daughters in research like this, navigating the same tug-of-war with their own mothers. They haven't forgotten that. They're trying to discern how to manage things well with their own daughters, but sometimes it still comes off poorly.

That is the boundary conversation in a nutshell. A daughter may be focused on protecting her time, energy, and independence. Her mother is at a stage of life when she is intensely focused on family ties. She's laser-focused on keeping the relationship close, but maybe doesn't have the skills to make it happen, just the desire for it to be so. Both daughter and mother are responding to real needs. They just aren’t the same needs.

And nowhere does that mismatch become more visible than during the holidays, when traditions, expectations, and family identities are on full display.

As a family communication researcher, I’ve spent more than a decade studying the invisible work of daughtering: the task, emotional, cognitive, and identity labor adult daughters do to keep families connected. Lately, I’ve become especially interested in what happens when daughters begin to renegotiate that work.

Boundary conflict isn’t really about what a daughter is willing to do or a wall she's putting in place with her mother. The tension is about what these boundaries end up meaning to everyone else. A daughter's work (or lack thereof) ripples to every corner of the family. When she decides to prioritize some needs more than others and set down some of the unnecessary labor she's been doing, expect the family to shift, either seismically or gently, but it will change nonetheless. But you should know, daughter, you have every right not to abandon yourself and your needs. Set the boundary, but don't be shocked when others dislike it or feel hurt. Wait it out with empathy and gentle understanding. A new paradigm is on the horizon.
