item.title: When We Forgive, What New Meaning Do We Find in Life?
item.description:
Forgiveness

When We Forgive, What New Meaning Do We Find in Life?

Have you embraced any of the 6 meanings described here after you have suffered?

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • After we suffer and then forgive, we have the opportunity to find new meaning from these experiences.
  • To find meaning is a cognitive exercise, related to the behavioral goals of exercising new purposes in life.
  • Have you had a chance to examine the new meanings you now have with others as a result of such suffering?

Suffering could lead to despair, depression, hopelessness, and even not liking oneself (Yu et al. 2021; Reed & Enright, 2006). Yet one aspect of the forgiveness process, especially as one nears the end of the forgiveness journey, is the sometimes surprising development of finding meaning in that suffering and a new purpose in life. Finding meaning centers on an important question: What have I learned from going through this suffering, and what have I learned as I walked the journey of forgiveness? This is a cognitive exercise that can lead to new short-term and long-term goals (Enright, 2015). In other words, the cognitive exercise of finding meaning can lead to behaviors that support new purposes in one’s life.

Source: Dizain777 / Dreamstime

The psychotherapist and Holocaust survivor, Viktor Frankl (1969/2014), pioneered this idea of finding meaning in suffering as he endured the persecution of his imprisonment. His motivation was to resist being destroyed by the abuse. By finding meaning, one can transcend suffering and make it more bearable.

When I discuss the theme of finding meaning in suffering through forgiveness, I am not focusing on the injustice but on its aftermath. The basic question is this: What are you learning about life as you extend mercy to those who were deeply unfair to you? This post explores the different meanings people tend to generate as they forgive.

Let us first start by examining what finding meaning in suffering is not, because it can be misunderstood.

What Finding Meaning in the Context of Forgiveness Is Not

Consider three themes that sometimes are confused with finding meaning in what an unjustly acting person has done to the forgiver.

First, the forgiver is not denying the disappointment, sadness, anger, or grief in what was suffered. The injustice did happen, and the negative response is real. In other words, finding meaning is not some kind of non-feeling, interpreted, at least temporarily, as relief from the effects of the injustice.

Source: Yuri Arcurs /Dreamstime

Second, the person does not play games with themselves, stating, for example, “Oh well, things happen for a reason, and I’ll just make the best of it by accepting it.” Yes, people can “make the best of it,” but if this is an exclusive meaning of suffering, the one who forgives is not going after the woundedness inside, which may linger for a long time. The “oh well” approach is passive. To heal from the effects of the injustice, a person needs a more active approach to the pain.

Third, the forgiver does not distort reality by thinking, “Well, all things happen for good reasons, and so I will try to see the good in what happened to me.” The injustice was not good. Some aspects of what happens after the injustice may be good, but the injustice itself is not.

What Does Finding Meaning in Suffering Within Forgiveness Look Like?

Consider six points on this question.

1. Being more sensitive to the suffering of others, even those who never hurt you: James, upon forgiving, realized he had what he called a “short temper,” in which he imposed his anger on unsuspecting others. He has now committed, for example, to being more patient and kind to cashiers in grocery stores and pharmacies as he waits in line. He is more sensitive to the fatigue and stress of those working behind the cash register. This gives him a new sense of purpose, as he recognizes his intemperance in these contexts and now works to overcome his anger.

Source: Info723783 / Dreamstime

2. Being motivated to help others in their suffering: When Dr. Freedman (Freedman & Enright, 1996) worked with female incest survivors on a long-term forgiveness intervention, she saw that many of them, upon forgiving, became motivated to help other incest survivors overcome their deep resentment. They were not choosing as a goal to become mental health professionals, but instead to be of assistance to others who have suffered as they have.

As another example, I talked with a man who is imprisoned for life. Upon forgiving those who abused him, he said to me that he knows he will never get out of the correctional institution, but now he is motivated to help his cellmates forgive and to be unburdened of their anger. This led to a new purpose, or the behavioral manifestation of this desire to assist others.

3. Standing in the pain so you do not throw that pain onto others: The paradox of standing in the pain is this: As people bear the negative effects of unjust treatment by not throwing that pain back to the offending person or to unsuspecting others, the pain-bearers realize they are stronger than they thought. They see the positive outcomes of not seeking revenge. As Gandhi said, if we keep taking an eye for an eye, the whole world will be blind. The pain-bearers realize they can now translate this into a new purpose of contributing to a more peaceful world.

4. Forgiving helps us think more deeply about justice: If people are continually treated unjustly, they can find meaning in living a life of mercy and fairness integrated together. Thus, their understanding of justice can become wiser, and therefore their appropriation of justice can become more helpful to others.

5. Eventually, you can develop an overall philosophy of life, such as committing to be a conduit of good in this world: This is what Dr. Frankl called supra-meaning, or a new philosophy of life that encompasses an overall approach to how one interacts with others and why one does so in this way. For example, a person can commit to living a life of greater respect, kindness, and love toward both offenders and others. For example, Sally decided to resist impatience and negative emotions toward her own children, as a way of life in her family, so that these life-giving moral virtues can become norms there.

6. As people find meaning in their suffering, they can put their future purpose in life into sharper perspective: Finding meaning, in other words, becomes the cognitive rationale and emotional motivation to seek what matters to them.

In summary, our suffering is not for nothing. People who suffer and forgive can develop as they think carefully about what they are learning about suffering, their own humanity, and life itself. As Dr. Frankl learned and passed his wisdom on to us, finding meaning in suffering opens unexpected doors for survival and growing in our humanity.

item.title: Why Autistic Employees Are Targeted By Bullies
item.description:
Autism

Why Autistic Employees Are Targeted By Bullies

How organizations can support psychosocial safety for all neurotypes.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Autistic employees are more likely to be bullied and less likely to be believed or helped.
  • Traditional anti-bullying processes put the burden on targets, which may further harm bullied employees.
  • Prevention by design, through transparency, civility with voice, and just processes protects everyone.
Gossiping coworkers
Source: RiaKartika / pixabay

Workplace bullying damages health and drains productivity. For autistic employees, it perpetuates the cycle of abuse that starts much earlier. A 2026 review confirmed that autistic students experience disproportionately high levels of bullying, with most estimates falling between 40% and 70% (Heredia-Oliva et al., 2026), and it is a major source of stress for them.

The painful pattern then follows people into work. And many work environments prove fertile grounds for both overt (threatening, shouting) and especially covert (backstabbing, sabotaging) types of bullying (Praslova et al., 2022).

Why workplace bullies target autistic people: reasons, excuses, and no reasons at all

In experiments, neurotypical observers reported liking autistic people less than other neurotypical people, with vague explanations like perceived “awkwardness” (Alkhaldi et al, 2021). Workplace stressors have the potential to magnify the dislike. Autistic employees, with their spiky profiles of abilities, are more likely to be on extreme ends of performance. High performers often experience veiled violence like sabotage or having crucial information withheld due to coworker envy; struggling performers face overt hostility, which makes their performance further decline (Jensen et al., 2014). Add autistic tendencies of direct communication, including possibly challenging inefficiencies and misconduct (Hartman & Hartman, 2024), along with a focus on work over socializing, and the target is set.

Why autistic people are more likely to suffer deeper harm

Autistic people's nervous systems often have less capacity to recover from social stress (Cheng et al., 2020), and autistic adults are already at elevated risk of developing mental and physical health issues due to a mismatch between their needs and the environments, sensory stress, effortful masking, and other forms of chronic stress (Botha & Frost, 2020; Dhanasekara et al., 2023). Past bullying also leaves a psychological trace. My school expereince was such that the sound of laughter made me shudder, and in a research study, 87.4% of autistic adults showed signs of fear of being laughed at, compared with 22.6% of non-autistic adults (Leader et al., 2018).

Multiple vulnerabilities create compounding effects. Years of mistreatment result in hypervigilance and keep the body's threat response switched on. Each new injury is a blow to a system that never fully recovered from the last. To make things worse, the lack of resources often associated with unemployment, with only about 3 in 10 working-age autistic people in the UK employed (Buckland, 2024), leaves fewer options for recovery, seeking help, or leaving a toxic job.

Why autistic people might be less likely to get help

Reporting bullying at work is generally a thankless task. Reports are often ignored or dismissed: in a nationally representative U.S. survey, 60% of employers reacted negatively when bullying was reported (Namie, 2021), and targets describe HR as regularly siding with bullies (Boddy & Boulter, 2025). Moreover, skillful manipulators, which many bullies are, can present themselves as victims.

Autistic people, however, face additional barriers to successfully reporting bullying and being heard.

  • First, autistic people are less likely to be believed. Autistic adults telling the truth are judged less credible than non-autistic adults (Lim et al., 2022), partly because avoiding eye contact and fidgeting are incorrectly interpreted as signs of lying. In addition, in most modern societies, cultural norms are such that autistic reports of their own expereince are discounted in favor of neurotypical interpretations - a case of epistemic injustice.
  • Second, autistic people are less likely to receive empathy. Non-autistic observers form less favorable impressions of autistic people within seconds, a bias driven by reactions to external characteristics like communication style (Sasson et al., 2017). And while misunderstanding and the difficulty of forming a connection may run both ways (Milton, 2012), power doesn't, so an allistic bully's account is likely to feel more relatable to an allistic manager.

Why traditional responses to bullying fail

Most organizations say they are committed to healthy workplaces, but their methods for handling bullying often make things worse. Those methods fail autistic employees and others dealing with trauma or overwhelm in at least three ways.

They are reactive. Action typically begins only after bullying is proven. But the first line of defense against bullying and any other hazard at work is prevention (Praslova et al., 2022). Preventing harm is both more ethical and more practical than repairing it.

They put the burden on the target. Targets are told to document what was said and done, when, and who was present, then discuss it calmly with a supervisor. How many people can realistically do this while doing their jobs, under stress, and dealing with trauma? The process appears to be designed to make it easy to reject the complaint because of the “tone” or the target “being emotional.”

They try to fix personalities. Bullies may act out their entitlement, fragile egos, and poor self-control, but bullying flourishes where the environment lets it go undetected and rewards it with resources or advancement (Praslova et al., 2022; Salin, 2003). Trying to change personalities is not an effective way to produce sustainable organizational change.

Prevention by design

Fixing environments is a more productive way to positively change norms and behavior than attempting to change humans (Praslova, 2024). Here are a few mechanisms, described in more detail in Praslova et al., (2022) and Praslova, (2024).

Remove the rewards for bullying. Avoid internal competition for scarce resources. Distribute resources fairly and transparently, and balance individual rewards with team rewards. Realistic workloads reduce bullying used to offload work onto others, and transparency may take some of the fuel out of envy. Transparent decision-making makes rumors and backstabbing less likely to pay off (Praslova et al., 2022).

Set standards and train for them. A clear policy should state that bullying is not tolerated, and name its covert forms, not just its overt ones (Praslova et al., 2022). Train everyone in respectful communication, and train new managers specifically for complex interpersonal situations. Ideally, facilitate professional support from psychologists trained in workplace well-being.

Build civility and voice together. Some people mistake authenticity for a license to be cruel. Others try to buy “calm” by silencing people. Neither works. Understanding the four climates that emerge when civility and voice are combined can support the most functional organizational environment (Praslova, 2019):

  • Constructive (high civility, high voice): people can ask questions and raise sensitive issues without fear, as long as they avoid personal attacks. This climate best supports clarity, well-being, and productivity.
  • Contentious (low civility, high voice): people speak freely but carelessly, and rudeness may become acceptable.
  • Compliant (high civility, low voice): an illusion of peace that is fertile ground for covert bullying such as gossip, backstabbing, and withholding information.
  • Corrosive (low civility, low voice): frustrated, fearful employees turn on each other, overtly and covertly.

Breaking the Cycle

Bullying of autistic people is a predictable outcome of systems that fail to check assumptions, reward sameness and conformity, and make targets prove their own reality. Workplaces that are healthy by design, with transparency, civility, and voice, on the other hand, not only support autistic people, but make work better for everyone (Praslova, 2024).

This article builds on prior Specialistene blog entries and my book, The Canary Code: A Guide to Neurodiversity, Dignity, and Intersectional Belonging at Work.

item.title: When It's Always All About "Me"
item.description:
Identity

When It's Always All About "Me"

Why our relentless self-focus often makes us suffer.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • From a young age, we are taught to recognize ourselves as a "me."
  • As we grow older, we experience life through a "self" lens, focusing primarily on how events affect us.
  • Self-help can exacerbate this self-focus, frequently causing us to feel unhappy and insecure.

This is Part 1 of a multi-part series.

We’re living in the age of “me.” We see most things through the lens of “self”: How’s this experience going for me, and how am I doing? What does this mean for and about me? How’s this person perceiving me? Does my “me” like this or not? Our culture teaches us to be the protagonist of our life, make something of ourselves, be “somebody”—to actualize and optimize ourselves. We should be exceptional, the “star” of our own story, hero of our own journey.

Source: AI-Generated / ChatGPT

From the moment we can gaze into a mirror, those around us start saying, “That’s you!” “Look at you!” “There you are!” We start being recognized (and celebrated) as a “me,” a “someone” who’s her own unique identity, the one doing this life. A few years later, we learn to advocate for and protect that “me,” snatching toys from other little people, saying “That’s mine,” “Give me my…” We build a sense of possession, of being a “me” who has things or doesn’t.

Soon after (and for the rest of our life), we take on the project of that “me” and start working on behalf of our “me.” We become our own protector, PR rep, agent, and biographer, the narrator of our self-story—the story of “me.”

So too, the message we learn is that this “me” must be moving forward in life, continually progressing towards some better future version of ourselves, a new-and-improved, happier-and-better “me.” We can never rest because we must continue stacking up evidence of our advancement. As we are and where we are, we’re not enough—our “me” still hasn’t done enough. There’s some place, or so we’re taught, at the end of all our progress, where we will have progressed far enough and become enough to make the project of “me” complete, and set it down. Then we’ll be able to experience life directly without our “me” in the way.

We don’t just nurse at the bottle of progress; we also feed on the narrative of materialism, which offers us a system of values and ideas about what “counts” as progress. As the narrative goes, money, success, power, and lots of shiny things will earn us the elusive enough-ness we seek, and the right to stop focusing on our progress and the project of “me.” The problem is that this promised place of enough-ness, where we can finally stop protecting ourselves and progressing on our hero’s journey, never comes. No matter how much we achieve and prove about our worth, enough-ness eludes us, so we must continue pursuing the advancement of our individual “me.”

The self-help market is built around this same premise: that the individual is a project to be continually improved. The message is that our “me” needs to be fixed, or at the very least, needs to be better than she is. We’re supposed to be living more authentically, manifesting the life we deserve, putting ourselves first, distinguishing ourselves, and always becoming our best self (which is definitely not this self).

Self-help teaches us to relentlessly focus on our own experience and how we’re doing in every moment—how our life is going, and, most importantly, how the project of “me” is going. We learn to gauge and evaluate the present moment by whether it gives us what we want and need, whether it’s “good” for us. While paying attention to our own experience and how the present moment is affecting us is profoundly important and necessary for a healthy person, as is the ability to honor one’s own wants and needs, the problem is that this self we’ve learned to place at the center of our attention and indeed existence becomes the operating system through which we experience all of life. We don’t experience life directly, what’s actually happening; we experience what our life says about us, which we also invent and create in our mind.

Does this situation, interaction, or opinion make me feel good about me? Do I feel safe, secure, liked, important as a result of it? Does it support my self-image, the story I tell myself about myself? Am I getting what I need to shore up the version of myself I need to function? We encounter, experience, and react to life through a self-referencing lens, as a reflection of and commentary on who we are.

At the same time, our self-focus is motivated by our most basic instinct: survival. On an evolutionary level, we’re always trying to protect our existence as a species—to stay alive, continue being. Long ago, when we lived in the forest, we had to focus on threats: other animals that might eat us or our offspring, branches that could land on our heads, a dark sky that meant our nest would be flooded. Seeing reality through the lens of how it would impact our survival—through the lens of “me” and mine has deep biological roots.

And indeed, statistically, it made more sense to pay attention to what could kill us than what could delight us, like finding a great berry to eat. This now translates into “negativity bias,” our tendency to focus on what’s negative over what’s positive. But threats in modern times are generally not branches or other animals, but rather threats to our ego, self-esteem, and the grand story of who we are. In everyday life, it’s the psychological front on which we now feel continually endangered. It’s our “me” that has to constantly be on the lookout for danger.

All this to say, we have many good reasons to put ourselves at the center of the universe, and to see life through a personal lens of what it means for and about “me.”

The irony, however, is that our constant self-focus and the effort we put into shoring ourselves up, protecting and proving our self, promoting the “story” of our self, is actually an attempt to make ourselves feel happy and secure. And yet, it ends up making us feel unhappy and insecure. In the system we’ve designed, the relentless defense and hyper-vigilance to the self’s survival can never end. But in fact, it can… we just need to step out of the system.

In part 2, I’ll illuminate the subtle and not-so-subtle suffering that our “me” lens creates. I will also propose a radical solution. Spoiler alert: it will go against everything you’ve ever learned.

item.title: The Spectrum of Family Estrangement
item.description:
Family Dynamics

The Spectrum of Family Estrangement

4 ways family distance can happen, even if you're still speaking.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Family estrangement exists on a spectrum, from emotional distance to no contact.
  • Regular contact with family does not guarantee emotional closeness.
  • Structured or low contact can help preserve relationships while maintaining boundaries.
  • Estrangement can involve grief and loss while creating space for healthier relationships.

They say to write what you know. For better or worse, I know this topic from both sides of the couch.

A 2025 YouGov survey found that 38 percent of American adults reported being estranged from at least one immediate family member (Orth, 2025). When you hear the word estrangement, you may think of Hollywood-style relational pyrotechnics, with family members storming out of the house, never to speak to one another again.

To be fair, that does happen. But estrangement isn’t always about screaming fights and punishing silence. Researcher Kristina Scharp (2019) describes family estrangement as a continuum involving multiple dimensions, including emotional closeness, communication, physical distance, and the desire for reconciliation.

Here are four ways family estrangement can show up.

1. Emotional Estrangement

Proximity is a factor that can contribute to closeness, but is insufficient by itself. You can live near your family, see them every week, or even reside under the same roof, but physical proximity doesn’t guarantee emotional intimacy. More simply put, seeing your family regularly doesn’t mean that you share emotional closeness with them.

2. Structured Contact

With structured contact, the relationship remains intact, but you have a non-negotiable list of rules that need to be in place in order to avoid conflict either interpersonally or intrapsychically. You still maintain contact, but you’ve established limits around when, where, and how interactions happen. Structured contact may look like time limits when attending family gatherings, staying in a hotel instead of with your family, or limiting conversations to topics that don’t escalate. Structured contact can provide a way to maintain a connection while reducing exposure to harmful dynamics.

3. Low Contact

With low contact, you may have rules about how and when to engage, or you may find yourself stuck in the same conversational loops on repeat. With low contact, you limit your exposure to family to only the minimum amount necessary to “check the box” of spending time with family. Low contact can often be a healthy way to preserve what remains available in a family, or it can be a way to mitigate the guilt and shame that come when you go full no contact.

4. No Contact

No contact is exactly what it sounds like. There are no phone calls, emails, texts, or visits. No contact with family can run counter to deeply held beliefs about family connection, and many people agonize for years or even decades before they do it. Contrary to public opinion, going no-contact with family is not simply a trend, and ethical psychotherapy involves carefully exploring the reasons for considering estrangement rather than encouraging it without thoughtful consideration.

Research by Reczek et al. (2023) found that periods of parent-child estrangement can be followed by renewed connection. When all parties involved are committed to the change process, even long-standing periods of estrangement may find their way toward repair. Often, when repair fails to be an option, it’s because one or more parties may be unwilling or unable to participate in the process.

The decision to estrange yourself from family, regardless of which level of estrangement is appropriate, is one that is best made with informed supporters. Sometimes, estrangement isn’t even a choice, but the consequence of another family member’s rejection or withdrawal. While it can be a grief-laden experience, and one that should never be taken lightly, estrangement can also open up possibilities for loving and reciprocal relationships that do not cost you your energy or well-being.

item.title: How Long Does Heartache Last?
item.description:
Relationships

How Long Does Heartache Last?

Recovery from post-breakup symptoms is influenced by many factors.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Post-dissolution distress is unpleasant yet common after a breakup.
  • Many factors affect how quickly a person will recover from post-breakup symptoms.
  • A longer relationship, being left (versus leaving), and having poor coping strategies make recovery harder.
Source: by simarik from Getty Images Signature

Ending a romantic relationship can be heartbreaking. Whether you initiated the breakup or were dumped by the love of your life, most people experience some distress when a romantic relationship ends. This leads many people living through a painful breakup to ask: How long will my heartbreak last?

Common Post-Breakup Symptoms

Post-dissolution distress is a general term used to describe the unpleasant yet common mental health symptoms people report after a breakup (Dailey et al., 2024). Some of the most commonly reported symptoms include:

  • Strong negative emotional states and reactivity (e.g., feelings of sadness, despair, anxiety, anger, fear, guilt or disgust; being easily triggered)
  • Preoccupation and cognitive impairment (e.g., preoccupation with the ex; excessive rumination; unwanted intrusive thoughts; memory or concentration problems)
  • Engaging in unhelpful or problematic behaviors (e.g., stalking or cyberstalking/monitoring of ex; impulsive or compulsive efforts to contact the ex)
  • Physiological or somatic complaints (e.g., shifts in eating and sleep; low energy or fatigue; increased blood pressure)
  • Identity-based concerns (e.g., existential questioning of life purpose; loss of personal value without the ex)
  • Stress-related responses (e.g., related to change in housing, routines, friends, finances, child-rearing)

For some people, post-breakup symptoms are mild in intensity and subside over time. In a longitudinal study of 156 young adults assessed before, during, and after a romantic breakup, for example, Acolin and colleagues (2023) found an increase in depressive symptoms immediately following a breakup that generally returned to pre-breakup levels within three months.

However, others experience intense, impairing, longer-lasting symptoms that are sometimes associated with depression, anxiety, and other diagnosable mental health conditions (Field, 2025). In an important longitudinal study completed over 30 weeks, Verhallen and colleagues (2022) examined depressive symptoms following a romantic breakup in 87 women. Results yielded four distinct trajectories for post-breakup symptoms: a ‘resilience’ group who recovered most easily; a ‘fast recovery’ group who experienced distress but recovered; a ‘slow recovery’ group who improved but continued to struggle; and a ‘chronic distress’ group who did not improve significantly over time.

Factors That Affect Breakup Recovery

Not all romantic breakups will result in intense distress and some individuals are more vulnerable to symptoms than others (Dailey et al., 2024; Farber et al., 2024; Fernandes et al., 2025; Gehl et al., 2024). Many factors can influence the intensity of post-breakup symptoms including:

  • Relationship characteristics. In the months immediately following the end of a relationship, having a positive view of an ex, higher relationship ratings before the breakup, cohabitating, being financially dependent/interdependent, and being left (versus leaving) are generally associated with greater post-breakup symptoms.
  • Psychological characteristics. Having poor coping skills, lower self-esteem, and relational anxiety/insecurity are associated with stronger symptoms.
  • Insecure attachment style or experiencing child maltreatment. Generally being uncomfortable trusting or being emotionally close to others in a healthy way is associated with strong breakup symptoms.
  • Demographic factors. Being younger and experiencing a first breakup (often found in high school or college samples) is often associated with stronger breakup symptoms.

The Naked Truth

Although short-term post-dissolution distress is common for anyone going through a breakup, some people struggle with more intense, longer-lasting symptoms. Having a positive view of one’s ex; living together or having plans for a future; having poor coping skills, lower self-esteem, or an insecure attachment style; being youngerr; and being left (versus leaving) tend to make symptoms worse.

The good news is that breakups also provide an opportunity for growth, learning, and self-exploration. In a study of 1846 adults in the United States recruited to explore how psychotherapy facilitates coping, for example, Farber and colleagues (2024) found that 74.6% of the sample attended psychotherapy after a breakup and found it moderately to very helpful. Getting social support by talking to friends, ending contact with the ex, engaging in hobbies or work, finding a good therapist, and writing or journaling about the breakup experience facilitates post-breakup recovery and healing.

item.title: Recovering From Stress: 4 Strategies Leaders Need Now
item.description:
Leadership

Recovering From Stress: 4 Strategies Leaders Need Now

Are leadership stressors dragging you down? Learn tips to turn things around.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Being a leader is stressful, but you can recover effectively if you use the right techniques.
  • Disconnecting from technology helps with recovery.
  • Relaxing or engaging in a hobby you are passionate about assists in recovery.
  • Taking control of your boundaries, tasks, or schedule facilitates recovery.

Every leader wants to know the answer to the question: “How can I de-stress when leading takes a toll on me?” But while you might want to change things about your actual workday, it can be hard to control what happens when you’re “on the clock.” The good news—recovery after work can make a big difference in how you feel the following day. This is helpful because you can better control your recovery when you’re at home.

But you have to be strategic about how you approach recovery. Different approaches have different outcomes. Today, we highlight four key strategies that are needed for recovery from your workday.

Detachment Aids Recovery

Detachment is the feeling that you are mentally removed from work. This means that you aren’t engaging in work tasks or thinking about work-related issues. We have talked about the importance of detaching from technology after work before. This is key because it might prompt you to engage in work tasks (e.g., answering an email) or it might encourage you to think about problems or issues you’re facing at work.

There are other ways to detach as well. If you find yourself constantly talking about work at home, or dwelling on interactions with coworkers or clients, you may need to do a better job of monitoring your thoughts and actions. Even if technology isn’t interrupting your off-work time, you can sometimes interrupt your own downtime. Overall, if you’re thinking about or doing work when you’re trying to recover, you’re defeating the purpose.

If you really want to recover, you need to unplug from your work, mentally and physically.
Source: Markus Winkler/Pexels

Relaxing Is a Must for Recovery

We have all promised ourselves that we were going to relax—and then broken that promise—before. Relaxation, particularly in today’s demanding culture, seems selfish. But relaxation is necessary if you want to be able to perform better the next day.

When you’re at work, especially if your job is stressful, your body is in a state that is “activated.” In order to combat this activation, you need to introduce some activities that stop that activation and allow the body to rest. Otherwise, you’ll be in constant “go mode,” which can result in negative health outcomes in the future.

In other words, your body needs rest, and your mind needs a break. Relaxation can also help your brain detach from negative emotions and produce more positive emotions. This is important for the same reason. If your body is constantly in a state of stress, you will burn out. So, you need activities that make you feel happy, as a counterbalance. Relaxation can occur from taking a leisurely walk in nature, listening to music, meditating, or enjoying nice scenery, among other things.

Aim for Mastery When You Can

While the goal of relaxing is to kick back and unwind, there are also positive recovery benefits of tackling interesting challenges outside of work. When you take a pottery class, achieve a fitness goal, or learn a new language, your mastery goal is activated. So, if you’re interested in something, spending time on it helps you recover. This means that a balance between relaxation and mastery might be ideal.

For example, you might spend 30 minutes meditating and then spend some time learning to knit. Both of these activities would help with your recovery, even though one is more passive and the other is more active. Achieving a difficult goal that is important to you can also make you experience more positive emotions. So, while it might seem nice to just “veg” out, don’t forget those activities that make you feel like you’re progressing toward being the person you want to be!

Engaging in a hobby you're passionate about is great for recovering!
Source: cottonbro studio/Pexels

Recovery Requires Control

We have discussed the importance of autonomy at work before. Turns out, it’s important to have control over your recovery as well. Being able to dictate how you spend your time out of work can have important consequences for your health. In fact, people who have less control at home tend to be more depressed in the long term. So, it’s important to have conversations with family and friends about what you’d like to do in your “downtime” and to work with them to achieve it.

This means that if your friend is dying to take a creative writing class, but it stresses you out, you might need to turn down the offer. Similarly, if you love yoga but your family always seems to interrupt, you might need to find strategies to communicate the importance of this activity to your well-being. Overall, people like to be in charge of themselves and their day. When it comes to recovery, things are no different.

Conclusion

Research has shown that using all four of these strategies is the most effective way to decrease emotional exhaustion, increase your ability to perform at work and in life, and boost your physical health. But if you can only use one, that’s better than nothing! Try to start small by increasing your recovery in the area that resonates most with you. What will you do to detach, relax, master your goals, or control your recovery this week? Write it down or put it on your schedule—and stick to it!
